title: Using async/await Inside Array.prototype.forEach
symptoms: Asynchronous operations inside forEach finish out-of-order, and subsequent code runs before loop tasks complete.
roast: Flipping every lever at once and wondering why the TNT cannon fired backwards into your own face.
diagnosis: forEach does not await the Promises returned by its callback function; it executes synchronously and immediately returns undefined.
debuggingSteps: Replace forEach with a standard 'for (const item of items)' loop for sequential execution
Use Promise.all(items.map(async item => ...)) for concurrent execution
Check return values of async loops
whyItWorks: A native 'for...of' loop awaits each iteration before proceeding, guaranteeing synchronous sequential execution.
tests: const res = []; for (const x of [1, 2]) { res.push(await Promise.resolve(x)); } assert.deepStrictEqual(res, [1, 2]);

title: IEEE 754 Floating-Point Precision Equality Failure (0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3)
symptoms: Conditional check '0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3' evaluates to false, causing unexpected logic failure.
roast: Counting three emeralds and the villager insists you only gave him 0.30000000000000004 emeralds.
diagnosis: JavaScript numbers are 64-bit IEEE 754 binary floats. Decimal numbers like 0.1 cannot be represented precisely in base 2, accumulating small rounding inaccuracies.
debuggingSteps: Compare difference with Number.EPSILON: Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON
Multiply by scale factors (e.g. cents instead of dollars) to perform integer arithmetic
Use a precision math library like decimal.js or BigInt for monetary figures
whyItWorks: Number.EPSILON represents the difference between 1 and the smallest floating point number greater than 1, accommodating binary rounding variance.

title: Loss of Execution Context ('this') in Unbound Callbacks
symptoms: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined when accessing this.property inside a method passed as callback.
roast: Handing your dog collar to a villager and expecting the dog to sit when the villager yells.
diagnosis: Extracting an object method and passing it as a callback decouples it from its parent object. At invocation time, 'this' defaults to undefined (in strict mode) or window/global.
debuggingSteps: Use an arrow function wrapper: () => obj.method()
Explicitly bind in constructor: this.method = this.method.bind(this)
Declare the class method as an arrow property: method = () => { ... }
whyItWorks: Arrow functions lexically bind 'this' to the enclosing instance context at creation time.
tests: class C { v = 1; get = () => this.v; } const c = new C(); const fn = c.get; assert.strictEqual(fn(), 1);

title: Implicit Type Coercion Hazards with Loose Equality (==)
symptoms: Unintended equality evaluations like '0 == false' or '[] == false' lead to bypasses in authentication or validation logic.
roast: Accepting dirt blocks as gold ingots just because they're both stackable: check your trade receipts.
diagnosis: Loose equality ('==') invokes complex implicit type coercion rules according to ECMAScript specifications, converting operands to common primitive types before checking value.
debuggingSteps: Always use strict equality ('===') and strict inequality ('!==')
Enable ESLint rule 'eqeqeq: ["error", "always"]'
Coerce types explicitly when type conversion is intentional (e.g. Number(str) === 0)
whyItWorks: Strict equality ('===') checks both type and value without performing any implicit type conversion.

title: Closure Capturing Hoisted 'var' in Asynchronous Loops
symptoms: Callbacks scheduled in a loop all print the final loop index instead of their respective step indices.
roast: Naming 3 tame wolves in a loop, but all of them answer to 'Wolf #3' because 'var' forgot to create new tags.
diagnosis: 'var' declarations are function-scoped, not block-scoped. All callbacks capture a reference to the same single hoisted variable.
debuggingSteps: Replace 'var' with block-scoped 'let' in the loop initialization
Avoid 'var' declarations in modern ES6+ codebases
Use Array.prototype.forEach or IIFE if targeting legacy environments
whyItWorks: 'let' creates a new lexical binding for each loop iteration, ensuring every closure captures its own independent index value.
tests: const res = []; for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { res.push(i); } assert.deepStrictEqual(res, [0, 1, 2]);

title: Crash from Unhandled JSON.parse SyntaxError on Invalid Input
symptoms: SyntaxError: Unexpected token in JSON at position 0 causes unhandled server or client crash.
roast: Throwing a raw iron ore into a crafting table and expecting it to instantly produce armor.
diagnosis: JSON.parse throws a synchronous SyntaxError if the input string is empty, undefined, malformed, or HTML error pages from broken network responses.
debuggingSteps: Wrap JSON.parse in a try/catch block
Provide a fallback default object on failure
Create a safeParse helper utility function
whyItWorks: Enclosing the parse attempt in a try/catch block intercepts the SyntaxError and returns a safe fallback.
tests: function p(s) { try { return JSON.parse(s); } catch { return null; } } assert.strictEqual(p('bad'), null);

title: Unintentional Object Mutation via Reference Sharing
symptoms: Modifying an object inside a function unexpectedly changes the caller's state in other components.
roast: Handing your buddy your map, and he scribbles all over it: now your copy is ruined too.
diagnosis: Objects and arrays in JavaScript are passed by sharing (reference). Modifying object properties inside a function mutates the original object in memory.
debuggingSteps: Use object spread ({ ...obj }) or structuredClone(obj) for pure functions
Treat inputs as immutable parameters
Use Object.freeze() in development to catch mutation attempts
whyItWorks: The spread operator shallowly clones properties into a new object, leaving the input object intact.
tests: const orig = { a: 1 }; const updated = { ...orig, b: 2 }; assert.strictEqual(orig.b, undefined);

title: Array.prototype.sort Default Lexicographical Ordering on Numbers
symptoms: [10, 5, 2, 1].sort() produces [1, 10, 2, 5] instead of numeric ascending order.
roast: Sorting your chests by alphabetizing the number of diamonds: now 10 diamonds ranks lower than 2 diamonds.
diagnosis: By default, Array.prototype.sort converts elements to strings and compares UTF-16 code unit values, ordering '10' before '2'.
debuggingSteps: Always supply a numeric comparator callback: arr.sort((a, b) => a - b)
For descending order: arr.sort((a, b) => b - a)
Remember that sort() mutates the array in-place; use arr.toSorted() if non-mutating is required
whyItWorks: A numeric comparison callback subtraction (a - b) returns a negative, zero, or positive value instructing the sort algorithm on mathematical order.
tests: const n = [10, 5, 2]; n.sort((a, b) => a - b); assert.deepStrictEqual(n, [2, 5, 10]);

title: Returning Undefined from Arrow Function with Block Body {}
symptoms: Array.prototype.map produces array of [undefined, undefined, ...] when curly braces are added.
roast: Putting ingredients into a furnace with a closed door and walking away before lighting the fire.
diagnosis: In arrow functions, concise body (no braces: x => x * 2) returns implicitly. Block body (with braces: x => { x * 2 }) requires an explicit return statement; otherwise it returns undefined.
debuggingSteps: Remove curly braces if returning a single expression: (x) => x * 2
Or add the 'return' keyword inside braces: (x) => { return x * 2; }
Wrap object literals in parentheses: (id) => ({ id })
whyItWorks: An explicit return keyword directs the JavaScript execution engine to pass the calculated value out of the function block.

title: Unhandled Promise Rejections Crashing Node.js Process
symptoms: Process crash with 'UnhandledPromiseRejection: This error originated either by throwing inside of an async function without a catch block...'
roast: Ignoring a zombie banging on your wooden door until it breaks in and ends your hardcore run.
diagnosis: In Node.js 15+, unhandled Promise rejections terminate the process with non-zero exit code by default instead of issuing a warning.
debuggingSteps: Chain .catch() on every un-awaited Promise chain
Enclose await expressions inside try/catch blocks
Register process.on('unhandledRejection', handler) as a safety net
whyItWorks: Attaching a .catch() callback attaches an error rejection handler, satisfying the unhandled rejection safety monitor.
tests: let caught = false; Promise.reject(new Error('err')).catch(() => { caught = true; }); await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 10)); assert(caught);
